title: The black stone
hook: pilgrims kiss, touch or point to it, as the Prophet ﷺ did

segments.voice: Yesterday, tawaf, seven circuits, and your line: around the center. What was the still thing you came back to? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-six.

Umar ibn al-Khattab walks up to a corner of the Ka'ba, bends toward a dark stone set into the wall, and kisses it. Then he straightens up and speaks to it. The words are kept in Sahih al-Bukhari, and they're blunt. I know you are a stone. You can neither harm nor help. If I had not seen the Prophet kiss you, I would not have kissed you. Today, the stone, and why a man who said all that still bent down to it.
screen: `UMAR KISSES THE STONE.` → `I KNOW YOU ARE A STONE.` → `ONLY BECAUSE THE PROPHET DID.`

segments.voice: First, where it is. The black stone is set into one corner of the Ka'ba, and that corner is where each circuit of yesterday's tawaf begins and ends. Second, Umar's words, and what they guard against. He says out loud the thing someone watching might wonder about: is this stone a power? No. It can't harm and it can't help. Whatever honor it has comes from one place, that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ honored it. So the kiss isn't worship of a stone. It's following a person, in a small physical way, exactly as he did. Third, the crowds. Today, getting close enough to kiss the stone can mean a long, hard push through a packed crowd. And here another report in Bukhari helps. Ibn Abbas says the Prophet once went around the House riding a camel, and whenever he came to the corner, he pointed to it and said Allahu akbar. He didn't get down. He didn't push. He pointed. So pilgrims have three ways: kiss it if you can reach it, touch it with a hand, or, from a distance, raise a hand toward it and say God is greatest. Fourth, what that means for the crowd. In this report, the pointing isn't a fallback. It's the Prophet's own way that day. Nobody needs to shove an old man aside to honor a stone that, in Umar's words, can't help anyone. A raised hand from far back in the crowd is a full greeting. A salute to the corner, and the circuit goes on.
screen: `THE CORNER WHERE EACH CIRCUIT BEGINS.` · `IT CAN NEITHER HARM NOR HELP.` · `KISS, TOUCH, OR POINT.` · `THE RAISED HAND IS A FULL GREETING.`

segments.voice: The practice: point toward the qiblah. Find which way Mecca lies from where you are; a phone compass or a prayer app can tell you. Turn to face it. Then, slowly, raise your right hand toward it, the way a pilgrim does from far back in the crowd. If you pray, you can say Allahu akbar, God is greatest, quietly. If you don't, just hold the gesture for a breath and notice the distance it crosses. Then lower your hand, settle, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
The black stone. The stone in the corner of the Ka'ba that pilgrims kiss, touch, or point to, as the Prophet did. Today's word.
Your line: a salute to the corner. Today, when you can't get close to something you care about, find the small gesture from where you stand, and make it. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: During tawaf, pilgrims begin each circuit at the black stone; those who can reach it kiss or touch it, and others raise a hand toward it from a distance and say Allahu akbar.

fork.setup: you're Umar, standing at the black stone. people are watching. what do you do?
options: kiss it, then say aloud it's only a stone, kissed because the Prophet kissed it.
fork.reveal: he kisses it, then tells it: it can neither harm nor help, and he'd not have kissed it had he not seen the Prophet do so.

original.note: the black stone, in the corner of the Ka'ba.

trapdoor: what you thought: a holy rock people kiss.
what it means: a corner stone honored only because the Prophet honored it; kiss, touch or point.
what a scholar hears: Umar's words in Bukhari draw the line between following the Prophet and venerating a stone.

notes: Bukhari 1597 (Umar: 'I know you are a stone, you neither harm nor benefit...'): paraphrased; confirm number.

Bukhari 1613 (Ibn Abbas: the Prophet circled on a camel, pointing to the corner and saying takbir each time): confirm number (also 1612). Bukhari's wording mentions pointing 'with something he had'; the script says 'pointed'.
'Umar's sentence has kept that line clear for anyone who's read it since' and 'a long, hard push through a packed crowd': general color; check.
Practice: raising the right hand toward the qiblah outside tawaf is an imitation, not a rite; Keeper to check the framing is respectful.

Editor: fixed the order in Bukhari 1597: Umar kisses the stone, then speaks ('I would not have kissed you'); hook screen, fork and reveal follow; cut unsourced 'kept that line clear' and softened 'not a lesser version'.
